a: A prayer of a person in misery
t: A title that names a situation, not a person
p: The only psalm title that describes the one praying instead of naming an author. Any sufferer can step into it.
b: Most titles name a singer (David, Asaph, the sons of Korah) or an event. This one names a condition: tefillah le'ani, "a prayer of (or for) the afflicted one," "when he faints away." It reads like a note in a prayer book telling the user when to pray it. The psalm itself mixes a sick person's lament (102:1–11, 23–24) with hope for Zion's rebuilding (102:12–22), so many scholars think a personal prayer was later fitted to the nation's ruin in the exile, or that the sufferer speaks as one of Zion's ruined people. The church counted Psalm 102 among the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), a list Cassiodorus already used in the 500s.
r: Psalm 6:0; Psalm 32:0; Psalm 51:0; Psalm 130:1; Psalm 143:1; Psalm 142:2

a: pours out his troubled thoughts before the LORD
p: Hebrew Bibles count this title as verse 1, so each Hebrew verse number is one higher. The Greek calls it Psalm 101.
b: This site, like most English Bibles, numbers a psalm's title as verse 0. Hebrew Bibles count the title as verse 1. In Psalm 102 the title is a full line, so English 102:25 is Hebrew 102:26. In Psalm 103 the title is one word, "of David," and shares the first Hebrew verse, so the numbers agree; Psalms 104 to 106 have no titles. The Greek and Latin Bibles also number the psalms themselves differently: Psalms 102 to 106 are Psalms 101 to 105 there, the numbers used in Orthodox service books and older Catholic Bibles. Siach, "troubled thoughts," is the inner talk of a worried mind, the same word Hannah uses for her trouble (1 Samuel 1:16).
orig: וְלִפְנֵי יְהוָה יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ (velifne YHWH yishpokh sicho)

a: my bones are scorched like a hearth
p: The sufferer burns with fever. The word for "hearth" may mean a fireplace or the glowing coals in it.
b: Moqed is a burning place, a hearth or the embers on it. Together with "smoke," "dried up" and "bones stick to my flesh" (102:5), the images describe a body wasting with fever and hunger. Lament psalms often describe sickness through the bones (Psalm 6:2; Psalm 22:14; Psalm 31:10; Psalm 32:3). Lamentations uses the same pictures for Jerusalem after its fall (Lamentations 1:13; Lamentations 4:8), which is one reason scholars hear the ruined city in this personal prayer.
orig: כְּמוֹ־קֵד (kemo-qed), Leningrad Codex; many manuscripts כְּמוֹקֵד

a: for I have forgotten to eat my food
p: The Hebrew says simply "I have forgotten from eating my bread": grief and sickness have taken away all appetite.
b: Lechem is bread, and so food in general. Fasting in grief was normal in Israel (2 Samuel 12:16–17; Psalm 35:13), but this is not a chosen fast. The sufferer is so worn down that eating no longer comes to mind. Then in 102:9 his only "bread" is ashes. Hannah, too, "would not eat" in her distress (1 Samuel 1:7).

a: I am like the owl of the open wilderness
p: The two birds named here (qa'at and kos) are unclean birds of ruins. Older Bibles guessed "pelican."
b: Qa'at and kos appear in the list of unclean birds (Leviticus 11:17–18; Deuteronomy 14:16–17), and the prophets put the qa'at in deserted cities (Isaiah 34:11; Zephaniah 2:14). The Greek has "pelican" and "night raven," and the KJV followed with "pelican of the wilderness," though pelicans are water birds. Most modern scholars think both are owls or similar birds that haunt ruins. The point is clear whatever the species: the sufferer is like a creature that lives alone among broken walls ("rubble," charavot), a picture that again fits Zion in ruins.
orig: קְאַת מִדְבָּר ... כּוֹס חֳרָבוֹת (qe'at midbar ... kos charavot)

a: use me in their curses
p: Literally "they swear by me": his enemies hold him up as a warning, "May you end up like him."
b: To "swear by" someone here means to use his fate as the model of a curse. Jeremiah says the exiles' names will be used the same way: "May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab" (Jeremiah 29:22, a fresh rendering). Isaiah 65:15 and Numbers 5:21 show the same custom. The sufferer has become a byword, as the nation became one among the peoples in exile (Deuteronomy 28:37).
orig: בִּי נִשְׁבָּעוּ (bi nishba'u), 'by me they swear'

a: you picked me up and flung me away
p: God lifts the sufferer up and hurls him aside: a picture of rejection, not of chance illness.
b: The sufferer does not explain his illness as bad luck or as an attack by demons, as some neighboring prayers did. He traces it to God's "rage and anger," without naming any sin. That is why many readers put Psalm 102 with Job and Lamentations: God is both the one who has struck and the only one who can heal. The verb shalakh (Hiphil) is used for throwing away something worthless (Jeremiah 22:28).

a: My days are a shadow stretching out at evening
p: A shadow stretches longest just before the sun sets and the shadow vanishes. His life is nearly over.
b: Tsel natuy, a "stretched-out shadow," is the long shadow of late afternoon, just before dark. The image is the opposite of God's own permanence, which the next verse begins: "But you, LORD, sit on your throne forever" (102:12). The same contrast between fading human days and God's endless years shapes the end of the psalm (102:23–27), and Psalm 103:15–17 and Psalm 90:5–6 make it too.

a: But you, LORD, sit on your throne forever
p: The psalm turns from "I" to "you." God sits as king, and his name is remembered in every age.
b: We'attah, "but you," turns the prayer three times: here, in 102:26 ("but you will stand") and in 102:27 ("But you are he"). "Sit" (yashav) means sit enthroned, as in Psalm 9:7 and Psalm 29:10. The second line nearly repeats Exodus 3:15, where God's name is his "remembrance" for every generation, and Lamentations 5:19 has almost the same line at the end of its laments over Jerusalem.
orig: וְאַתָּה יְהוָה לְעוֹלָם תֵּשֵׁב (ve'attah YHWH le'olam teshev)

a: Yes, the hour you set has come
p: The psalm expects a set time for Zion's restoration, as Jeremiah's "seventy years" did.
b: Mo'ed is a set time, the same word as for festivals. Here it is the time God fixed for showing Zion favor. Many scholars connect it with the prophetic count of the exile, Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11; Jeremiah 29:10), which Daniel 9:2 and 2 Chronicles 36:21 also take up. The singer prays from the ruins (102:14) and believes the end of the punishment has come. Isaiah 40:1–2 announces the same moment: Jerusalem's hard service is over.

a: For your servants take delight in her stones
p: God's servants love even the broken stones and dust of Zion. The city lies in ruins.
b: This is one of the plainest signs that the psalm comes from the time after Jerusalem's fall in 587 or 586 BC. The stones are the rubble of the city and temple; the dust is what is left. Sanballat mocked the builders: "Will they bring stones back to life out of piles of dust, and burned stones at that?" (Nehemiah 4:2), and Lamentations mourns the stones of the holy place poured out at every street corner (Lamentations 4:1). Jewish tradition kept this love for the ruins: the Talmud tells that Rabbi Abba kissed the rocks of Akko out of love for the land, and Rabbi Hiyya bar Gamda rolled in its dust, citing this verse (Bavli Ketubot 112a–b).

a: The nations will be in awe of the LORD's name
p: When God rebuilds Zion, the kings of the earth will see his glory, a hope shared with Isaiah 40–66.
b: The psalm moves from one person's illness to the whole world. When the LORD has built Zion and "has been seen in his glory" (102:16), the nations and their kings will fear him, and peoples and kingdoms will gather to serve him (102:22). The prophets of the return say the same: "the LORD's glory will be uncovered, and all people together will see it" (Isaiah 40:5, a fresh rendering; compare Isaiah 59:19; Isaiah 60:1–3). Psalm 102 joins the hope of a rebuilt city with the hope that the nations will worship Israel's God.

a: those stripped bare
p: The rare word 'ar'ar means "stripped" or "destitute." Jeremiah uses it for a bare desert shrub.
b: Ha'ar'ar appears only here as a word for people. Jeremiah 17:6 uses it of a scrubby plant in the desert, probably a juniper, and Jeremiah 48:6 has a similar word. It comes from a root meaning "to strip bare." So the people whose prayer God hears are those with nothing left, like a city whose walls have been stripped (the same root in Jeremiah 51:58). The title's "person in misery" (102:0) and "those stripped bare" here are the same people.

a: will praise Yah
p: Yah is the short form of God's name YHWH. This part writes it "Yah," as the site's Exodus 15:2 does.
b: The Hebrew here is yehallel-Yah, "will praise Yah." Yah is the short form of the name YHWH, used in poetry (Exodus 15:2; Psalm 68:4) and heard in hallelu-yah, "praise Yah." The site writes the short name "Yah" where it stands alone, and renders the full name "the LORD." The cry hallelu-yah itself is rendered "Praise the LORD!" (104:35; 105:45; 106:1; 106:48).

a: a people that will be created
t: A people yet to be created
p: God will "create" a new people, using the verb of Genesis 1. The psalm is written down for readers still to come.
b: Am nivra uses bara, the verb kept in the Bible for God's own creating (Genesis 1:1). The restored community will be something God makes new, as in Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 43:7; Isaiah 43:21, where God "created" Israel "for my glory." The verse also says why the psalm was written down: "for the next generation." It is a prayer kept for later readers, and the Psalter itself is that kind of book. The last word is yehallel-yah, "will praise Yah," the short form of the divine name found in "Hallelujah."
r: Genesis 1:1; Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 43:7; Isaiah 43:21; Isaiah 65:17–18; Psalm 22:30–31; Psalm 78:4–6

a: to unbind the children of death
p: "Sons of death" means people condemned to die. The prisoners may be exiles or people under sentence.
b: Bene temutah, "children of death," is a Hebrew way of saying "those doomed to die," like "a son of death" in 1 Samuel 20:31 (with a related word). Psalm 79:11 has nearly the same line about the prisoners and "the children of death," and in both places the prisoners are probably Israelites in exile or captivity. God looks down from heaven (102:19) to hear and free them, the way he "saw" and "heard" Israel's groaning in Egypt (Exodus 2:23–25; Exodus 3:7).

a: do not take me away
p: The verb means "take up" or "carry off": do not let me die young, with half my life still unlived.
b: Al-ta'aleni, "do not make me go up," is used of being taken away, as Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:1, a related use). The prayer is to live out a full life. "Half of my days" shows the ancient hope of a long life as God's blessing (Isaiah 38:10, Hezekiah's prayer in sickness, has "in the middle of my days"). The singer sets his short days against God's "generation after generation" of years, which leads into the hymn of 102:25–27.

a: Long ago you set the earth on its foundations
p: Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes 102:25–27 from the Greek and applies it to the Son: he founded the earth, and he remains.
b: Hebrews chains together seven scripture texts to show the Son is greater than the angels. One is this passage, introduced simply "And": "You, Lord, at the beginning laid the earth's foundation, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will be lost, but you stay on ... But you are the same, and your years will not run out" (Hebrews 1:10–12, a fresh rendering). Hebrews uses the Greek, which adds "Lord" and reads 102:23 differently, so that the words can be heard as God speaking to someone he calls Lord. Hebrews' "roll them up" (Hebrews 1:12) is found in Codex Vaticanus and a few other Greek copies, but the main Greek text has "change them," as the Hebrew does (see the variants). In the Hebrew the singer speaks to the LORD. Hebrews' point is that the Son shares the creator's role and the creator's permanence.

a: They will be lost, but you will stand
p: Heaven and earth wear out like clothes; God remains. Does the world end, or is it renewed?
b: The verse does not deny that God made the world firm (Psalm 104:5). It compares even the heavens to a coat that wears thin and gets changed for a new one. Isaiah 51:6 uses the same picture: "the heavens will scatter like smoke, and the earth will grow threadbare like clothing" (a fresh rendering), and Isaiah 65:17 promises new heavens and a new earth. Many Jewish and Christian readers take this as renewal, a change of clothes rather than a destruction. Others, with 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 21:1, read it of a real ending followed by a new creation. Either way, the psalm's comfort is not the world's permanence but God's: "you will stand."
r: Isaiah 51:6; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 65:17; Matthew 24:35; 2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1; Psalm 104:5

a: But you are he
p: Atta hu, "you are he," echoes God's own "I am he" in Deuteronomy 32 and Isaiah. It means God is always the same.
b: The Hebrew is two words, atta hu. In the Song of Moses God says, "I, only I, am he" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and in Isaiah he says "I am he" of his lasting identity: "I am the LORD, first of all, and with the last ones too, I am he" (Isaiah 41:4, a fresh rendering; compare Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 46:4). The Greek turned it into "you are the same" (su de ho autos ei), which Hebrews 1:12 quotes and Hebrews 13:8 echoes: "Jesus Christ, yesterday and today the same, and to the ages" (a fresh rendering).
r: Deuteronomy 32:39; Isaiah 41:4; Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 46:4; Hebrews 1:12; Hebrews 13:8; Malachi 3:6

a: Your servants' children will settle down and stay
t: An ending in the next generation
p: The sufferer may die young, but the servants' children will live in the land. The psalm ends in hope for others.
b: The psalm does not end with the sufferer healed. It ends with God's servants' descendants living securely "in your presence," that is, in the land and near the temple. This is the same hope that ends Psalm 69 (Psalm 69:35–36) and that the exiles held: if not we, then our children. Christian readers have also heard here the church that lives on because the Son remains (Hebrews 1:10–12). Jewish readers have read it of Israel's survival through every exile.

a: Bless the LORD, my soul
p: To "bless" God is to praise and thank him, telling him how good he is. The singer talks to his own soul.
b: When God blesses people, he gives them life and good things (Genesis 1:28). When people "bless" (barakh) God, they cannot give him anything; they speak well of him with gratitude. Some versions translate "Praise the LORD" here, which loses the link with the many blessings God gives. The singer speaks to his own nefesh, his soul or whole living self, and even to his "insides" (qeravay). The Hebrew verbs and pronouns in 103:1–5 are feminine because nefesh is a feminine noun: the singer is preaching to himself.
r: Psalm 104:1; Psalm 104:35; Psalm 34:1; Psalm 16:7; Genesis 1:28; Psalm 42:5

a: Bless the LORD, my soul
t: Five times "Bless the LORD, my soul"
p: The Talmud counts five uses of this call in Psalms 103 and 104 and links each to a way the soul is like God.
b: Psalms 103 and 104 both open and close with "Bless the LORD, my soul" (103:1, 2, 22; 104:1, 35). The Talmud asks why David said it five times and answers with five comparisons: as God fills the world, the soul fills the body; as God sees but is not seen, so does the soul; as God feeds the world, the soul feeds the body; as God is pure, the soul is pure; as God lives in the innermost room, so does the soul. Therefore, it says, let the soul, which has these five things, praise the one who has them (Bavli Berakhot 10a).

a: He pardons every wrong you have done
p: The list of God's gifts begins with forgiveness, then healing, rescue from death, and a crowned and satisfied life.
b: The verbs in 103:3–5 are participles, "the one who pardons, the one who heals, the one who ransoms, the one who crowns, the one who fills," like titles of God. Salach, "pardon," is used in the Bible only with God as the one who forgives. Putting pardon and healing side by side reflects the common belief that sickness could follow sin (Psalm 41:4; compare Exodus 15:26, "I am the LORD, your healer"), but the psalm does not say each illness is a punishment. The New Testament joins the two when Jesus forgives and heals the paralyzed man (Mark 2:5–12).
r: Exodus 15:26; Psalm 41:4; Psalm 107:17–20; Isaiah 33:24; Mark 2:5–12; James 5:15

a: He ransoms your life from the Pit
p: Ga'al is the verb of the family redeemer. The Pit (shachat) is the grave and the world of the dead.
b: Ha-go'el, "the one who ransoms," is the word for a family redeemer who buys back a relative (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:4). Here God is the family member who pays to bring the singer back from shachat, the Pit, another name for the grave and Sheol (Psalm 16:10; Psalm 30:9). Most readers take it as rescue from a deadly illness. The crown that follows turns the rescued sufferer into a kind of king: dressed in God's hesed, loyal love, and rachamim, tender mercy.
r: Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:4; Psalm 16:10; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 30:9; Job 33:28; Isaiah 43:1

a: He fills your years with good things
p: The Hebrew 'edyekh normally means "your ornament." Translators guess "your years," "your desire" or "your mouth."
b: 'Edi elsewhere means jewelry (Exodus 33:4–6; Jeremiah 2:32), which does not fit well here. Some scholars connect it with a root for "duration," so "your years" or "your prime"; the New JPS has "in the prime of life." The Greek reads "your desire" (see the variant), the KJV "thy mouth," following older Jewish guesses, and others suggest "your being" or emend the word. The Plain follows "your years," which fits the second line about youth, and marks the uncertainty here.

a: like the eagle, you grow young again
p: The eagle (or vulture) pictures strength renewed. Later readers told stories of how it grew young.
b: Nesher covers the great eagles and vultures. Isaiah 40:31 uses the same picture: those who wait for the LORD "will lift up wings like eagles" (a fresh rendering). Molting, when the bird grows new feathers each year, probably lies behind the image. Later readers made more of it. Medieval bestiaries told of an old eagle that flies up toward the sun and then plunges into a spring to be made young. Augustine, on this verse (his Psalm 102), retold a story that the old eagle's beak grows until it cannot eat, so it breaks the beak on a rock and feeds again, and he read the rock as Christ. The psalm itself says only that God's goodness makes the tired young again.

a: He let Moses know his ways
p: Moses asked, "let me know your ways" (Exodus 33:13). The psalm says God answered, and quotes what he showed him.
b: After the golden calf, Moses prayed, "let me know your ways, so that I may know you" (Exodus 33:13), and then, "Please let me see your glory" (Exodus 33:18). God passed in front of him and proclaimed his name: "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). Psalm 103:8 quotes that answer. So "his ways" here are not first of all the commandments but God's character, which he showed after Israel's worst sin. The rest of the psalm explains that character: he does not keep his anger (103:9), and he removes sins (103:12).

a: Compassionate and gracious is the LORD
p: This line quotes God's self-description in Exodus 34:6. It is the Bible's most repeated statement of who God is.
b: The words "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love" first appear when God proclaims his name to Moses (Exodus 34:6). Israel repeated them in prayer and preaching more than any other description of God: Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Psalm 86:15, Psalm 111:4, Psalm 145:8. Jewish tradition calls Exodus 34:6–7 the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and chants them on fast days and the High Holy Days. Psalm 103 quotes only the merciful half and leaves out "he will by no means leave guilt unpunished" (Exodus 34:7).
r: Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 145:8

a: He will not go on accusing without end
p: Riv means to bring a lawsuit. God is pictured as a plaintiff who could keep pressing charges but drops them.
b: Lo lanetsach yariv: "he will not forever bring a case." The prophets picture God bringing a lawsuit against Israel (Micah 6:2; Hosea 4:1). The second verb, natar, "keep, guard," is used for nursing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18; Jeremiah 3:5; Jeremiah 3:12). Isaiah 57:16 has the same promise: "Not forever will I bring charges, and not for all time will I be angry" (a fresh rendering).
orig: לֹא־לָנֶצַח יָרִיב וְלֹא לְעוֹלָם יִטּוֹר (lo-lanetsach yariv velo le'olam yittor)
r: Isaiah 57:16; Jeremiah 3:5; Jeremiah 3:12; Micah 6:2; Micah 7:18; Leviticus 19:18

a: As distant as the sunrise is from the sunset
t: As far as east from west
p: Hebrew names east and west by the rising and setting sun. The distance between them cannot be measured.
b: Mizrach is the place where the sun rises and ma'arav where it sets. The two horizons are as far apart as anything a person can see. Micah 7:19 uses a different picture for the same thing: God will throw all their sins into the depths of the sea. Isaiah 38:17 has "you have flung every sin of mine behind your back" (a fresh rendering).

a: The way a father feels tenderly for his children
p: Racham, the word for compassion, comes from the word for the womb. Here it is a father's feeling.
b: Rachamim, "compassion," is related to rechem, "womb," and Isaiah 49:15 uses it of a mother. Here the comparison is a father. The Hebrew Bible calls God Israel's father only a few times (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Jeremiah 31:9; Malachi 1:6), and always with this sense of care and loyalty. Jesus taught his followers to pray "Our Father" (Matthew 6:9). The tenderness is "for those who fear him": the phrase recurs in 103:11, 13, 17, describing the ones who live in reverent trust.
r: Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 63:16; Jeremiah 31:9; Hosea 11:1–4; Malachi 3:17; Matthew 6:9; Luke 15:20

a: he knows what we are made of
p: Yetser is what is formed, like a potter's clay. The rabbis later used it for the human inclination.
b: Yitsrenu, "our form," comes from yatsar, the potter's verb in Genesis 2:7: "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground." God remembers the dust he worked with. Later Jewish teaching used yetser for the impulses of the human heart, the good inclination and the evil inclination (from Genesis 6:5 and Genesis 8:21, "what the human heart shapes is evil"). Read with that later meaning, the verse says that God knows our weakness and makes allowance for it.
r: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21; Isaiah 29:16; Job 10:9; Psalm 90:3

a: A human being's days are like grass
p: The same picture appears in Isaiah 40:6–8, which 1 Peter quotes: people fade, God's word stands.
b: Enosh, the word for a human being here, often stresses weakness. Grass in the land of Israel greens after the winter rains and is burned brown by the first hot east wind (103:16). Isaiah sets the same fading grass against "the word of our God," which "will stand forever" (Isaiah 40:8, a fresh rendering), and 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes Isaiah. Psalm 103 sets it against God's hesed, which lasts "from long ago and on forever" (103:17).

a: its spot no longer recognizes it
p: A Hebrew idiom: after a person dies, their place forgets them. The same words appear in Job 7:10.
b: "Its place will not recognize it again" also occurs, nearly word for word, in Job 7:10, of a person who goes down to Sheol (compare Job 8:18). It is a strong way of saying that nothing is left behind. The "wind" (ruach) is the hot desert wind that withers grass in a day (Isaiah 40:7; Hosea 13:15).

a: from long ago and on forever
p: Luke 1:50, in Mary's song, echoes this verse: God's mercy lasts generation after generation for those who fear him.
b: Mary's song, the Magnificat, says: "His mercy is for generation after generation / of those who fear him" (Luke 1:50), echoing 103:17. Like Psalm 103, the song praises God for lifting the humble and keeping faith with Abraham's children (Luke 1:52–55). Me'olam ve'ad olam, "from long ago and on forever," is the phrase that closes Book IV (106:48).

a: In the heavens the LORD has set his throne firm
t: From one soul to the whole universe
p: The psalm widens step by step: from "my soul" to Israel, to all who fear God, to the angels and all creation.
b: Psalm 103 is built in widening circles. It begins with one person (103:1–5), moves to Israel and Moses (103:6–10), to all who fear God (103:11–18), and ends with God's throne in heaven and every angel, army and work everywhere under his rule (103:19–22). Then it comes back to where it began: "Bless the LORD, my soul." Many scholars note that this psalm has 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic; the number may suggest completeness, as in Lamentations 5.

a: His angels, bless the LORD
p: Mal'akhim are messengers, here angels. "Armies" (tseva'ot) are the heavenly forces of "the LORD of Armies."
b: The call widens to the heavenly court. Mal'akhav, "his messengers," are angels; they are "mighty in strength" and obey God's word the moment it is spoken. "His armies" (103:21) are the hosts of heaven, the stars and the angels, the same word as in the title "the LORD of Armies." "Servants" (mesharetav) is the word Psalm 104:4 uses of the fire. The human singer joins the angels' praise, a picture the church later used in the Sanctus, where earth sings with heaven (Isaiah 6:3; Revelation 4:8).
r: Psalm 148:2; Psalm 29:1; Psalm 104:4; Isaiah 6:3; Revelation 4:8; Hebrews 1:14

a: Bless the LORD, my soul.
t: A psalm without a title, paired with 103
p: Psalm 104 has no title in Hebrew; the Greek adds "Of David." It shares its opening and closing call with Psalm 103.
b: The Hebrew gives Psalm 104 no heading, but it opens and closes with the same words as Psalm 103 (103:1; 103:22; 104:35), and the collectors set the two side by side: 103 praises God the redeemer, 104 praises God the creator. The Greek (Greek Psalm 103) heads it "Of David" (Tōi Dauid), as it does several untitled psalms. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QPs-d places Psalm 104 after Psalm 147, and 11QPs-a puts it after Psalm 118, so its place in the collection was not fixed everywhere in the first centuries BC and AD.

a: You have dressed yourself in splendor and majesty
p: Splendor and majesty (hod and hadar) are a king's robes. God wears light the way a king wears his robe.
b: Hod vehadar is royal language (Psalm 21:5; Psalm 45:3). God's clothing is light (104:2), and the heavens are his tent (104:2), his upper rooms are built on the waters (104:3), and the clouds are his chariot. The first verses describe the King's house and travels before they describe the world he furnishes. Psalm 93:1 has the same picture: the LORD reigns, robed in majesty.
r: Psalm 93:1; Psalm 96:6; Psalm 21:5; Psalm 45:3; 1 Chronicles 16:27; Job 40:10

a: you spread out the heavens like a tent curtain
p: The psalm loosely follows the days of Genesis 1: light, sky, waters, land, plants, sun and moon, sea, people.
b: Read beside Genesis 1, the psalm moves in nearly the same order: light (104:2; Genesis 1:3), the heavens stretched out over the waters (104:2–3; Genesis 1:6–8), waters pushed back so the dry land appears (104:5–9; Genesis 1:9–10), plants and trees (104:14–17; Genesis 1:11–12), moon and sun for set times (104:19; Genesis 1:14–16), the sea with its creatures and Leviathan (104:25–26; Genesis 1:20–21, "the great sea monsters"), animals and people fed by God (104:21–23, 27–28; Genesis 1:24–30). But the psalm does not count days, mixes birds and animals throughout, and says nothing of the image of God or the Sabbath. Where Genesis says "God saw that it was good," the psalm prays, "let the LORD be glad in what he has made" (104:31). See the chapter page.

a: he turns the clouds into his chariot
p: Canaanite poems called the storm god Baal "Rider of the Clouds." The psalm gives the title to the LORD.
b: In the Ugaritic poems from about 1300 BC, Baal the storm god is called rkb 'rpt, "Rider of the Clouds." Israel's poets used the same picture for the LORD: Psalm 68:4 calls him "the one who rides through the desert plains" (some scholars read "on the clouds," as in the Ugaritic title), and in Psalm 18:10, "Riding a cherub, he flew"; in Deuteronomy 33:26 he rides the heavens. The verdict of most scholars: a real link of language, borrowed to make a claim. Rain, thunder and wind (104:3–4, 7, 13) belong to the LORD, not to Baal.
r: Psalm 68:4; Psalm 68:33; Psalm 18:10; Deuteronomy 33:26; Isaiah 19:1; Daniel 7:13

a: He makes the winds into his messengers
t: Winds as messengers, or angels made winds?
p: The Hebrew can mean "he makes winds his messengers" or "he makes his messengers winds." Hebrews 1:7 quotes the second.
b: The Hebrew reads, word for word, "making his messengers winds, his servants a fire blazing." Because Hebrew puts the two objects side by side, it can mean either that God turns winds and fire into his messengers, or that he turns his messengers (angels) into winds and fire. The context, a parade of nature serving God (104:3, 5), favors the first, which the Plain follows. The Greek took it the second way, "who makes his angels spirits (or winds)," and Hebrews 1:7 quotes the Greek to show that angels are servants who change form, while the Son's throne lasts forever (Hebrews 1:8). The Hebrew ruach means wind, breath and spirit.
orig: עֹשֶׂה מַלְאָכָיו רוּחוֹת מְשָׁרְתָיו אֵשׁ לֹהֵט ('oseh mal'akhav ruchot, mesharetav esh lohet)

a: it will not totter for ever and ever
p: This verse was once cited against a moving earth. Galileo answered that scripture speaks in everyday terms.
b: The psalm pictures the earth on solid bases that never shake, the way the world looks to a person standing on it (compare Psalm 93:1; 1 Chronicles 16:30). In the 1500s and 1600s, some opponents of Copernicus cited such verses as proof that the earth does not move. Galileo's Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615) answered that the Bible speaks of nature in ordinary language, citing Augustine at length and a saying he credited to Cardinal Baronius: the Holy Spirit meant to teach how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go. Today most Jewish and Christian readers agree that the verse praises the world's stability as God's gift, not its position in space. Psalm 102:26 shows the same poets could also say the heavens and earth will wear out.
r: Psalm 93:1; Psalm 96:10; 1 Chronicles 16:30; Psalm 102:25–26; Job 26:7; Job 38:4–6

a: The deep was the robe you put over it
p: Tehom, "the deep," is the same word as in Genesis 1:2. The waters once covered even the mountains.
b: Tehom is the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2: "Darkness lay on the face of the deep." Here it is pictured as a garment over the earth, with water standing above the mountains, before God's rebuke drove it into its place. Some readers have also heard the flood in these verses (Genesis 7:19–20, waters over the mountains; Genesis 9:11, never again), especially in 104:9: "they will not turn back to cover the earth." The Greek reads the line differently (see the variant).

a: When you scolded them, they ran
p: In many ancient stories a god defeats the sea in battle. Here God only shouts, and the waters run.
b: Babylonian and Canaanite poems tell of a storm god who must fight the sea: Marduk splits Tiamat in the Enuma Elish, and Baal defeats Yam ("Sea") in the Ugaritic Baal cycle. The Bible knows this language (Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 89:9–10; Isaiah 51:9–10). Psalm 104 keeps only a trace of it: God's ge'arah, "rebuke," and the voice of his thunder (compare Psalm 18:15; Psalm 106:9, where he shouts at the Sea of Reeds). There is no battle. The waters simply flee to the place he set for them, and the sea becomes a home for creatures (104:25). Most scholars see a real link, deliberately tamed; some, like David Tsumura, doubt that Genesis and the psalms depend on a battle myth at all.
r: Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 89:9–10; Psalm 18:15; Psalm 106:9; Isaiah 51:9–10; Job 38:8–11; Nahum 1:4

a: Up the mountains, down the valleys they went
p: The line can describe the waters running over mountains and down valleys, or the mountains rising and valleys sinking.
b: The Hebrew says "mountains go up, valleys go down, to the place you founded for them." Read with 104:7, the subject may still be the fleeing waters, which pour over the mountains and down into the valleys to their set place; the KJV reads it this way, and the Plain follows it. The Greek is ambiguous, since its nouns can be read either way, while the Latin makes the mountains and plains the subjects ("the mountains go up and the plains go down"). Others make "mountains" and "valleys" the subjects: as the water drained away, the mountains rose up and the valleys sank to the levels God founded for them. Both fit the picture of the dry land appearing (Genesis 1:9).
orig: יַעֲלוּ הָרִים יֵרְדוּ בְקָעוֹת (ya'alu harim yeredu veqa'ot)

a: You drew a line they will not pass over
p: God sets a limit for the sea. Job 38, Jeremiah 5 and Proverbs 8 use the same picture.
b: God speaks the same way to Job: "Up to here you may come, but not one step more" (Job 38:11). Jeremiah 5:22 makes the sand the boundary of the sea, and Proverbs 8:29 says God gave the sea its limit so that the waters would not pass his command. In the ancient world the sea stood for chaos. The boundary means the world is safe because God holds back what would undo it. The flood story is the one time the boundary was opened (Genesis 7:11), and the promise of Genesis 9:11 is that it will not be opened again.

a: the wild donkeys drink until their thirst is broken
p: The Hebrew says the wild donkeys "break" their thirst, as people still "break" a fast.
b: Yishberu fera'im tsema'am: the wild donkeys "break their thirst." The onager, the wild donkey of the steppe, is the Bible's picture of an animal no one can tame (Job 39:5–8; Genesis 16:12). Even this animal, which owes nothing to people, drinks from the springs God sends. In Psalm 104 the wild creatures are fed directly by God, not through humans.

a: so that bread comes up out of the ground
p: The three staples of the land: grain, wine and olive oil. God gives them through human work.
b: Grain, new wine and fresh oil are the gifts the covenant promises the land (Deuteronomy 7:13; Deuteronomy 11:14; Hosea 2:8). Here they come through "the work of human hands" ('avodat ha'adam), the same word for work or service that Genesis 2:15 uses for tending the garden. God makes the crops grow; people farm them; bread comes from the earth. Jewish blessing over bread uses the wording of this verse: "who brings out bread from the earth" (hammotsi lechem min ha'arets).

a: and wine that makes people glad at heart
p: The psalm praises wine as God's gift that gladdens people. Readers who drink and readers who abstain both cite it.
b: Wine here stands with bread and oil among God's good gifts (compare Judges 9:13; Ecclesiastes 9:7; John 2:1–11). The Bible also warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35; Ephesians 5:18). Christians who drink in moderation, including Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican tradition, point to this verse as proof that wine is a blessing. Many Methodist, Baptist and Pentecostal churches have urged total abstinence since the 1800s, and some of their writers argued that biblical "wine" was often unfermented juice, a view most scholars of the Hebrew reject for yayin.
r: Judges 9:13; Ecclesiastes 9:7; Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35; John 2:1–11; Ephesians 5:18

a: the cedars of Lebanon that he planted
p: No one planted the great cedars of Lebanon. They are "the LORD's trees," watered by him alone.
b: The cedars of Lebanon, up to about 130 feet tall, were the most valued timber of the ancient world. Egyptian, Assyrian and Babylonian kings boasted of cutting them, and Solomon's temple was built of them (1 Kings 5:6). The psalm calls them "the LORD's trees" because they grow in the mountains where no farmer waters them. Isaiah 14:8 imagines the cedars rejoicing when the king of Babylon, who cut them, falls.

a: the cliffs are where the rock badgers hide
p: The ye'elim are ibexes, wild mountain goats. The shephanim are hyraxes, small animals that live among rocks.
b: The Nubian ibex still lives on the cliffs at En-gedi ("spring of the young goat," 1 Samuel 24:2), and the rock hyrax, a rabbit-sized animal, lives among the rocks nearby. Proverbs 30:26 says the hyraxes are a people without strength, yet they make their homes in the crags. Older English versions called them "conies," and the Latin "hedgehogs"; the Greek has "deer" for the ibex and, for the hyraxes, the word it uses for the shaphan in Leviticus 11:5. Each creature in the psalm has its own place: birds in the trees, storks in the pines, ibex on the heights, hyraxes in the rocks.

a: He made the moon to keep the appointed times
p: Israel's calendar was lunar. The moon marks the mo'adim, the set feast days, as in Genesis 1:14.
b: Mo'adim, "appointed times," are the festivals of Leviticus 23, counted from the new moon. Genesis 1:14 also says the lights mark "the appointed times." The psalm names the moon first, perhaps because the Hebrew day began at sunset. Because of this verse, Jews recite Psalm 104 on Rosh Chodesh, the festival of the new moon, and in Ashkenazi custom also on Sabbath afternoons in the winter months. Notice that sun and moon are things God "made" with tasks to do. They are not gods, as they were in Egypt and Babylon.

a: You lay down the dark, and night comes
t: Psalm 104 and the Hymn to the Aten
p: An Egyptian hymn of about 1340 BC shares scenes with this psalm: night and lions, morning work, ships.
b: The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the tomb of Ay at Amarna under the pharaoh Akhenaten (about 1350–1334 BC), praises the sun disk. When the sun sets, it says, the land is dark as death, lions come out of their dens and snakes bite; at dawn people wake, wash and go to work, cattle graze, birds fly, ships sail up and down the river, and fish leap. It also cries out how many the god's works are (compare 104:24). Since James Breasted in the early 1900s, scholars have compared it with 104:20–30. The difference is as striking as the likeness. In the hymn, night is the sun god's absence and danger. In the psalm, God makes the dark (104:20), the lions ask God for their food (104:21), and the sun is only a creature that "knows where it sets" (104:19). See the chapter page.

a: they ask God for their food
p: The roaring of young lions is heard as a request to God. Every creature depends on him for food.
b: The verb "seek" (bakkesh) is used for prayer in the psalms (Psalm 27:8; Psalm 105:4). The psalmist hears the lions' roar as a kind of prayer, and God, not the hunt, provides. God asks Job, "Will you track down food for the lion / and fill up the young lions' bellies" (Job 38:39), and says the raven's chicks "call to God for help" (Job 38:41), and Jesus points to the birds that the heavenly Father feeds (Matthew 6:26). In this psalm even predators belong to God's good order.

a: Then a person heads out to his work
t: Night for lions, day for people
p: God divides time between the animals and people. The lions hunt at night; people work by day.
b: The psalm gives night to the wild animals and day to human beings. When the sun rises, the lions go home (104:22), and people go out. Human work is not a curse here, as it partly is in Genesis 3:17–19, but part of creation's rhythm, "until evening." The Egyptian Hymn to the Aten has a similar morning scene, with people rising, washing and dressing to go to work. In the psalm, people are one creature among many, not the crown of creation as in Genesis 1:26–28 and Psalm 8:5–8.

a: You made every one of them with wisdom
p: God made everything "with wisdom," like a skilled builder. Proverbs 8 pictures Wisdom beside God at creation.
b: Bechokhmah, "with wisdom," is the word for the skill of a craftsman such as Bezalel (Exodus 31:3). Proverbs 3:19 says the LORD founded the earth by wisdom, and Proverbs 8:22–31 gives Wisdom a voice: she was beside God as he set the boundaries of the sea, delighting in the inhabited world. Jewish readers later identified Wisdom with the Torah, and Christian readers with the Word, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The last word, qinyanekha, means "what you own" or "what you have made": the verb qanah means both "acquire" and "create" (Genesis 14:19).
orig: כֻּלָּם בְּחָכְמָה עָשִׂיתָ ... קִנְיָנֶךָ (kullam bechokhmah 'asita ... qinyanekha)
r: Proverbs 3:19; Proverbs 8:22–31; Jeremiah 10:12; Exodus 31:3; Genesis 14:19; John 1:3; Colossians 1:16

a: and Leviathan, which you shaped to sport in it
p: Elsewhere Leviathan is a monster God crushes. Here it is a creature God made to play in the sea, or to play with.
b: Leviathan is the many-headed sea dragon of Canaanite myth (Ugaritic Litan), whose heads God crushed (Psalm 74:14) and whom he will punish "on that day" (Isaiah 27:1). Job 41 describes it as a beast no human can tame: "Will you toy with it as with a pet bird?" (Job 41:5). Psalm 104 uses the same verb, sachaq, "play, sport," and the same boldness: the dragon is simply one of God's sea creatures, sporting in the waves near the ships. The Hebrew bo can mean "in it" (the sea) or "with him." The Talmud took the second: in the last part of each day, God plays with Leviathan (Bavli Avodah Zarah 3b). The Greek calls it "this dragon."
r: Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; Job 41:1–5; Job 3:8; Genesis 1:21; Revelation 12:3

a: They all wait on you
t: The eyes of all wait for you
p: Psalm 145:15–16 repeats this thought, and Jews and Christians have used it as a grace before meals.
b: Psalm 145:15–16 says nearly the same thing: "All eyes wait in hope for you, / and you hand them their food when it is time. / You open your hand / and fill every living thing with what it longs for" (Psalm 145:15–16). Jews say Psalm 145 (the Ashrei) three times a day, and verse 16 is the line at which many touch their tefillin. Christians, especially Lutherans, have used Psalm 145:15–16 as a table grace; Luther's Small Catechism gives it for that purpose. Psalm 104 adds the hard side: when God hides his face, the creatures panic and die (104:29).

a: You gather back their breath, and they die
p: The same Hebrew word, ruach, is the creatures' breath in 104:29 and God's breath or Spirit in 104:30.
b: Ruach means wind, breath and spirit. In 104:29 God "gathers back their ruach" and they return to dust, as in Genesis 3:19 and Ecclesiastes 12:7. In 104:30 he sends out "your ruach" and they are created. Life is borrowed breath. Job 34:14–15 says that if God gathered his spirit and breath to himself, all flesh would perish together. The Plain uses "breath" both times so the link is visible; most English versions write "Spirit" in 104:30 (see the note there).

a: You send your breath out, and they are created
p: Christians read this verse of the Holy Spirit, the giver of life, and sing it at Pentecost.
b: The Hebrew ruchakha can be translated "your breath" or "your Spirit." In the Hebrew Bible, God's ruach is his life-giving power, the same that hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2) and that revives dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9–14). The church heard the Holy Spirit here. The Latin Psalter has emittes, "you will send"; the liturgy turned it into the petition Emitte Spiritum tuum et creabuntur, et renovabis faciem terrae, the versicle of the prayer "Come, Holy Spirit," and Psalm 104 is the Catholic responsorial psalm for Pentecost. The Nicene Creed calls the Spirit "the Lord, the giver of life." Jewish readers take it as God's breath that renews each generation of creatures. "Created" is bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1: creation is not only a past event but goes on.
r: Genesis 1:2; Ezekiel 37:9–14; Job 33:4; John 20:22; Acts 2:1–4; Isaiah 32:15

a: let the LORD be glad in what he has made
p: Genesis says God saw that everything was very good. The psalm prays that God may go on rejoicing in his works.
b: Genesis 1:31 says: "God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good." The psalm turns that verdict into a wish: may God's glory last, and may he keep rejoicing in his works, and not need to shake the earth in judgment (104:32). Proverbs 8:30–31 pictures Wisdom delighting before God and in the inhabited world. The psalm ends not with humanity but with God's pleasure in everything he made, including the wild animals and Leviathan.

a: one touch on the mountains, and they pour out smoke
p: The trembling earth and smoking mountains recall Sinai, where God came down in fire and the mountain smoked.
b: At Sinai the mountain "smoked from top to bottom, since the LORD had come down upon it in the fire," and it quaked (Exodus 19:18). The same picture of God's coming appears in Psalm 144:5 ("touch the mountains and make them smoke"), Amos 9:5 and Micah 1:4. In a psalm about the order of creation, it is a reminder that the creator is also the holy one before whom the earth shakes.

a: Let sinners be finished off from the earth
p: The psalm's only harsh line. The Talmud tells how Beruriah read it as a prayer that sins, not sinners, would end.
b: The psalm's world has one flaw: the wicked, who do not fit God's good order. The singer prays that they "come to an end" (yittammu). The Talmud (Bavli Berakhot 10a) tells that Rabbi Meir was praying for some violent neighbors to die. His wife Beruriah pointed out that the word can be read chata'im, "sins," not only chot'im, "sinners," and that the next line says "and the wicked will be no more": when sins end, there will be no wicked people left. So he should pray for them to repent. He did, and they repented. The Hebrew letters in fact read chatta'im, which means "sinners" by its vowels but looks like "sins."

a: Praise the LORD!
p: This is the first "Hallelujah" in the Psalter. The Talmud noted that it first comes after the downfall of the wicked.
b: Hallelu-yah, "praise Yah," first appears in the Psalter here, and then often in Book V (Psalms 111–113, 146–150). The Talmud observed that David composed 103 psalms (counting Psalms 1 and 2 as one) before he said "Hallelujah," and that he said it only when he saw the downfall of the wicked, in this verse (Bavli Berakhot 9b–10a). The Greek moves the word to the head of the next psalm as a title (see the variant). Revelation 19:1–6 is the only place the word appears in the New Testament.
r: Psalm 105:45; Psalm 106:1; Psalm 106:48; Psalm 111:1; Psalm 150:6; Revelation 19:1–6

a: Give thanks to the LORD; call out his name.
p: Psalm 105:1–15 is also 1 Chronicles 16:8–22, the song David's singers sang when the ark came to Jerusalem.
b: Chronicles builds the song of 1 Chronicles 16:8–36 from three psalms: 105:1–15, most of Psalm 96, and 106:1 with 106:47–48. The Plain here uses the site's wording of 1 Chronicles 16 wherever the Hebrew is the same. The Hebrew differs in a few places: "seed of Abraham" here, "seed of Israel" in Chronicles (105:6; 1 Chronicles 16:13); "He keeps his covenant in mind" here, "Keep his covenant in mind" there (105:8; 1 Chronicles 16:15); "when they were" here, "when you were" there (105:12; 1 Chronicles 16:19); "anyone" here, "any man" there (105:14; 1 Chronicles 16:21); and small spellings (see the table on the chapter page). Chronicles turns a history psalm into a call to the people at the ark. Which came first is debated; most scholars think Chronicles drew on the psalms.

a: Let the peoples know his deeds
p: The psalm thanks God by retelling history from Abraham to the land. It may have been sung at a festival.
b: Psalm 105 is a hymn that tells history as praise. It speaks to "you seed of Abraham" (105:6), the worshiping people, and urges them to remember. Chronicles places its first part at David's bringing of the ark (1 Chronicles 16:7). Many scholars date the psalm after the exile, when its stress on the promise of the land (105:11, 44) and on God's protection of a small people among the nations (105:12–15) spoke to returned exiles. Others think it is older and was used at a covenant festival. Its partner Psalm 106 tells the same history as a confession of sin.

a: the rulings from his mouth
p: Mishpatim usually means legal rulings. Here, beside wonders and marvels, it means God's verdicts against Egypt.
b: The site renders mishpatim as "rulings" throughout. In 105:5 and 105:7, the rulings "from his mouth" that reach "the whole earth" are God's judgments in history, above all the plagues on Egypt, which Exodus also calls "judgments" (Exodus 6:6; Exodus 12:12). Only at the end of the psalm do the "rules" and "laws" of the covenant appear (105:45).

a: you seed of Abraham, his servant
p: "His servant" is Abraham; "whom he chose" is the sons of Jacob. Chronicles reads "seed of Israel."
b: In the Hebrew, "his servant" is singular and goes with Abraham (as in 105:42), while "his chosen ones" is plural and goes with Jacob's sons. The Greek and the Dead Sea scroll 11QPs-a make "servants" plural (see the variants). 1 Chronicles 16:13 has "seed of Israel," so that both lines name Jacob. Isaiah 41:8 joins the same titles: "you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, the one I chose, seed of Abraham who loved me" (a fresh rendering).

a: He keeps his covenant in mind for all time
p: In the Bible, for God to "remember" is to act on a promise. The psalm turns on God's remembering (105:8, 42).
b: Zakhar, "remember," does not mean God had forgotten. When God remembers Noah (Genesis 8:1), Abraham (Genesis 19:29), Rachel (Genesis 30:22) or his covenant (Exodus 2:24), he acts. The psalm opens with God remembering his covenant (105:8) and closes with him remembering "his holy word and Abraham his servant" (105:42). Between them, every event happens because of the promise. Chronicles, by contrast, makes it a command to the people: "Keep his covenant in mind for all time" (1 Chronicles 16:15). Zechariah's song in Luke 1:72–73 echoes this verse: God came "to keep in mind his holy covenant, the oath he swore to Abraham our father" (a fresh rendering).
r: Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24; Exodus 6:5; 1 Chronicles 16:15; 105:42; Luke 1:72–73; Psalm 106:45

a: what he agreed with Abraham
p: The promise of the land passes from Abraham (Genesis 15; 17) to Isaac (Genesis 26:3) to Jacob (Genesis 28:13).
b: The psalm names each step of the promise. God "cut" a covenant with Abraham, giving his offspring the land (Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:8). He swore to Isaac: "I will make good the oath that I swore to Abraham your father" (Genesis 26:3). He set it up for Jacob at Bethel: "The land you are lying on I will give to you and to your offspring" (Genesis 28:13). The psalm skips everything else in Genesis 12–36, such as Isaac's binding and Jacob's struggles, to make one point: the land was promised long before Israel owned it.
r: Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:7–8; Genesis 26:3; Genesis 28:13; Genesis 35:12; Hebrews 6:13–18

a: When they were men who could be counted
p: "Men of number" means men so few they could be counted. The ancestors lived in Canaan as foreigners.
b: The Hebrew idiom mete mispar, "men of number," means a small group, as Jacob says in Genesis 34:30: "I have only a few men." Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in Canaan as gerim, resident foreigners (Genesis 23:4; Genesis 26:3; Genesis 37:1), and moved among peoples: Canaanites, Philistines, Egyptians (105:13). For the exiles and returnees who sang this psalm, small and ruled by others, it was a picture of their own situation and of how God had protected such a people before.

a: he scolded kings because of them
p: God warned Pharaoh and Abimelech, king of Gerar, when they took Sarah (Genesis 12; 20; 26).
b: The kings are Pharaoh, whom "the LORD struck ... with great plagues over the matter of Sarai, Abram's wife" (Genesis 12:17), and Abimelech of Gerar, warned in a dream (Genesis 20:3–7; compare Genesis 26:11). In Genesis 20:7 God tells Abimelech that Abraham "is a prophet, and he will pray for you," which explains why the next verse calls the ancestors "my prophets."

a: Hands off my anointed ones!
p: The "anointed ones" are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The verse is often quoted to shield pastors from criticism.
b: No one poured oil on the patriarchs. "Anointed" (meshichay) is used in a wider sense of people God has set apart, and "prophets" fits Abraham (Genesis 20:7). The verse is sometimes quoted, "Touch not mine anointed" (KJV), to say that a pastor or preacher may not be questioned. In context it is God's protection of a small, landless family against kings who could have crushed them. The Greek translates christous, "anointed ones" or "christs." See the note on 1 Chronicles 16:22.

a: and snapped every staff of bread
p: Bread was the "staff" a person leaned on. To break it meant to cut off the food supply.
b: The idiom appears in Leviticus 26:26 and Ezekiel 4:16; Ezekiel 5:16; Ezekiel 14:13: God "breaks the staff of bread" in famine. The psalm says God "called" the famine, as if summoning a servant (compare 2 Kings 8:1). The story is Genesis 41–47: seven years of famine that "gripped" Egypt and Canaan (Genesis 41:54–57; Genesis 47:13). In the psalm, even the famine serves the promise, because it brings Jacob's family to Joseph.
r: Leviticus 26:26; Ezekiel 4:16; Ezekiel 14:13; Genesis 41:54–57; Genesis 47:13; 2 Kings 8:1

a: He had sent someone on before them
p: The psalm repeats Joseph's own reading of his story: his brothers sold him, but God sent him ahead.
b: The psalm takes its view from Joseph's words to his brothers: "God sent me ahead of you to keep a remnant alive for you on the earth" (Genesis 45:7) and "You were not the ones who sent me here; God was" (Genesis 45:8). It never mentions the brothers' jealousy or sale except in the passive "was sold" (Genesis 37:28; Genesis 45:5). Genesis 50:20 says the same: you planned evil, God planned it for good.

a: his neck went into iron
p: The Hebrew puts Joseph's neck (nefesh) in an iron collar. The Greek and Latin made it his soul.
b: Nefesh can mean throat or neck as well as soul or self, and here, with fetters on the foot, it is the neck in an iron collar. Genesis does not mention chains: it says Joseph was locked in the prison house (Genesis 39:20; Genesis 40:15). The Greek read "his soul passed through iron," the Latin ferrum pertransiit animam eius, and Miles Coverdale's psalter in the Book of Common Prayer turned it into "the iron entered into his soul," which became an English saying for deep suffering. It is a fine line, but not what the Hebrew says.

a: until the time his word came to pass
p: "His word" may be Joseph's dreams and interpretations, or God's word. Either way, waiting refined him.
b: "His word" can be Joseph's word, the dreams he told (Genesis 37:5–11) or his interpretation for the cupbearer (Genesis 40:12–13), which came true but was forgotten for two years (Genesis 41:1; Genesis 41:9–13). Or it can be God's own word or promise. The second line, "the LORD's saying refined him like metal," uses tsaraf, the verb for testing silver in fire (Psalm 12:6; Psalm 66:10). The Plain keeps the ambiguity. In both readings, the years in prison were the fire, and the word that finally came was God's timing.
r: Genesis 37:5–11; Genesis 40:12–13; Genesis 41:1; Genesis 41:9–13; Psalm 12:6; Psalm 66:10

a: He put him in charge of his household
p: Pharaoh's words in Genesis 41:40 lie behind this verse: "You will be in charge of my household."
b: Pharaoh says: "You will be in charge of my household, and all my people will obey your every word" (Genesis 41:40), and Joseph later says God made him "master of his whole house, and the one who governs all the land of Egypt" (Genesis 45:8). The psalm's "to tie up his officials as he wished" (105:22) is its own touch: Joseph, once bound, now has power to bind Pharaoh's officials. Genesis 41:44 makes the same point: "Apart from you, nobody in all the land of Egypt will move a hand or a foot."

a: and to make his elders wise
p: Joseph teaches Pharaoh's elders wisdom. Later Jewish writers made Joseph a model of Egyptian learning.
b: Genesis praises Joseph as "discerning and wise" (Genesis 41:39) but does not say he taught Pharaoh's court. The psalm adds it, perhaps from the wisdom tradition that saw Joseph as a sage. Later writers went further: Philo wrote a whole treatise on Joseph as the model statesman, and some Jewish writers in Greek, such as Artapanus as quoted by Eusebius, made Joseph a teacher of the Egyptians.

a: and Jacob stayed as a foreigner in Ham's land
p: Poetry calls Egypt "Ham's land" or "the tents of Ham," because Genesis 10 makes Mizraim (Egypt) a son of Ham.
b: Genesis 10:6 lists "Ham's sons" as "Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan," and Mizraim is the Hebrew name of Egypt. So the psalms call Egypt "the land of Ham" (105:23, 27; Psalm 106:22) or "the tents of Ham" (Psalm 78:51). "Stayed as a foreigner" (gar) is the verb of resident foreigners: Joseph's brothers told Pharaoh, "We have come to stay in the land as foreigners" (Genesis 47:4), as God had foretold (Genesis 15:13).
r: Genesis 10:6; Psalm 78:51; Psalm 106:22; Genesis 15:13; Genesis 47:4; Genesis 46:3–7

a: He turned their hearts toward hating his people
p: The psalm says God himself turned the Egyptians to hate Israel. Readers have asked how that fits God's goodness.
b: Exodus says a new king arose who did not know Joseph (Exodus 1:8) and feared Israel's growth (Exodus 1:9–12), and that God hardened Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 7:3). The psalm goes further and makes God the one who turned the Egyptians' hearts. Augustine and Calvin read it as God using hearts already inclined to evil for his purpose, without being the author of their sin. Many Jewish commentators (Radak, for example) explain that God let Israel's prosperity provoke Egyptian envy. Critical scholars see the psalm's theology at work: nothing in Israel's story happens outside God's plan.

a: They set out his signs among them
p: The psalm names eight plagues, not ten, in its own order, with darkness first.
b: Exodus 7–12 tells ten blows. Psalm 105 has darkness (Exodus 10:21–23), blood (Exodus 7:20–21), frogs (Exodus 8:6), the swarm and gnats (Exodus 8:17; Exodus 8:24), hail (Exodus 9:23–25), locusts (Exodus 10:13–15) and the firstborn (Exodus 12:29). It leaves out the livestock disease and the boils. Psalm 78:44–51 has a different list and order. Putting darkness first may make it a heading for the rest, or may reflect the poet's freedom. The plagues are "his signs" and "wonders," the same words as Exodus 7:3 and Deuteronomy 4:34.

a: and they did not defy his word
p: The Hebrew says "they did not rebel against his word." It is unclear who "they" are; the Greek drops the "not."
b: Readers have suggested several subjects. (1) Moses and Aaron, who obeyed in Egypt, unlike at Meribah, where God says "you rebelled against my word" (Numbers 20:24; Numbers 27:14). (2) The plagues themselves, which did what God commanded. (3) The Egyptians, who after the darkness no longer resisted, or who "did not keep" his word, if the verb is read shameru, "kept." The Greek and later Syriac readings say "they rebelled against his words," meaning the Egyptians (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Hebrew. The verb marah returns at 106:7, 33 and 43, of Israel's rebellion.
r: Numbers 20:24; Numbers 27:14; Exodus 10:21–29; Psalm 106:7; Psalm 106:33; Psalm 106:43

a: He spoke, and the swarm came on
p: 'Arov is a swarm of biting insects, probably flies. Kinnim are gnats or lice.
b: 'Arov (Exodus 8:21–24) means a mixture or swarm. The Greek called it kynomyia, "dog-fly," and the site's Exodus and Psalm 78:45 call it "the swarm." Kinnim may be gnats, mosquitoes or lice (Exodus 8:16–18). "He spoke, and ... came" (105:31, 34) echoes the creation formula, "God said ... and so it was" (Genesis 1:7; Genesis 1:9): the creator speaks, and creation obeys him against Egypt.

a: the first fruit of all their manhood
t: The first fruit of their manhood
p: A man's first son was called the first of his strength (Genesis 49:3). The last plague took the pride of every family.
b: Reshit lekhol onam, literally "the beginning of all their vigor," is Jacob's description of Reuben: "my strength and the first fruit of my manhood" (Genesis 49:3; compare Deuteronomy 21:17). Psalm 78:51 uses the same words. Exodus 4:22–23 explains the blow: "Israel is my son, my firstborn," and Pharaoh would not let him go.

a: He led them out carrying silver and gold
p: Israel left with Egypt's silver and gold, as God had promised Abraham and Moses.
b: Genesis 15:14 promises that Abraham's offspring "will come out with great wealth"; Exodus tells how the Israelites asked Egypt for silver things and gold things, "So they stripped Egypt bare" (Exodus 12:36). Some ancient and medieval readers saw this as back wages for slavery (Jubilees 48:18; Philo; and later Jewish commentators). No one "tripped" (koshel): Isaiah 5:27 uses the same word for an army in which no one stumbles.
r: Genesis 15:14; Exodus 3:21–22; Exodus 11:2–3; Exodus 12:35–36; Isaiah 5:27; Jubilees 48:18

a: He stretched a cloud over them for shelter
p: In Exodus the cloud leads the way. The psalm makes it a covering, like a tent roof over the people.
b: Exodus 13:21 has the pillar of cloud "to lead them along the road" by day and the pillar of fire "to light their way" by night. Psalm 105 has the cloud "spread" (paras) as a covering, a word used for spreading a tent or a wing. Isaiah 4:5–6 uses the same image for Zion's future: a cloud by day and fire by night as a canopy over it, a shelter from heat and storm. Paul says the ancestors "were all beneath the cloud" (1 Corinthians 10:1, a fresh rendering).

a: They asked, and in came the quail
p: In Exodus and Numbers the people grumble for food. Here they simply "ask." Psalm 106 tells the other side.
b: The Hebrew verb sha'al is singular, "he asked," with the people as a collective "he"; the Greek makes it "they asked." Exodus 16:3 and Numbers 11:4 tell the same events as complaining and craving, and Psalm 78:18 and 106:14–15 tell them as sin. Psalm 105 leaves the sin out on purpose: it is the psalm of God's faithfulness, and Psalm 106 is the psalm of Israel's unfaithfulness. "Bread from heaven" is manna (Exodus 16:4), which Jesus takes up in John 6:31–35.
r: Exodus 16:4; Exodus 16:13–15; Numbers 11:4; Numbers 11:31–34; Psalm 78:18–29; Psalm 106:14–15; John 6:31–35

a: He split open a rock, and the waters poured out
p: God brought water from a rock at Horeb (Exodus 17) and at Kadesh (Numbers 20). Paul says the rock was Christ.
b: Exodus 17:6 places the first miracle at Horeb: "You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it." Numbers 20:11 tells a second one at Kadesh, where Moses struck the rock twice. The psalm calls it a river through dry places (compare Psalm 78:15–16; Isaiah 48:21). Jewish tradition spoke of a well or rock that followed Israel through the wilderness, and Paul wrote, "they kept drinking from a spiritual rock that went along with them, and that rock was the Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4, a fresh rendering).
r: Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11; Psalm 78:15–16; Psalm 114:8; Isaiah 48:21; 1 Corinthians 10:4

a: He handed them the nations' lands
p: The psalm ends with the gift of Canaan, not with Israel's own conquest. It says nothing of Israel's failures.
b: The land came as a gift, the fruit of other peoples' labor, as Deuteronomy 6:10–11 says: cities you did not build, vineyards you did not plant. The psalm's history stops at the land and does not mention the judges, kings or exile. Jewish and Christian readers have debated what this promise means today: whether the land is still promised to the Jewish people, and whether the church inherits the promise in a wider sense (Hebrews 11:8–16; Romans 4:13). See the topic page on the Promised Land.

a: This was so that they would keep his rules
p: The whole history ends with its purpose: Israel was given the land so that it could keep God's rules and laws.
b: The order matters. God promised, protected, freed, fed and settled Israel before asking anything. Then comes the purpose: "so that they would keep (shamar) his rules (chuqqim) and guard (natsar) his laws (torot)." The Ten Words begin the same way: "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt" comes before "You must not" (Exodus 20:2–3). Deuteronomy 4:40 and Deuteronomy 6:20–25 link the gift of the land to keeping the commandments.

a: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good
p: This line opens Psalms 106, 107, 118 and 136, and Chronicles uses it as the Levites' song (1 Chronicles 16:34).
b: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; his loyal love is forever" is the best-known refrain of the temple. 1 Chronicles 16:34 quotes this verse without the opening "Praise the LORD!" Chronicles has the Levites sing it when the ark comes, at the temple's dedication and on the battlefield (2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; 2 Chronicles 20:21), and Ezra 3:11 at the new temple's foundation. Jeremiah 33:11 foresees it sung again in Judah's restored towns. Psalm 106 opens with it even though it goes on to confess a long history of sin, because the refrain says why there is still hope.
r: 1 Chronicles 16:34; Psalm 107:1; Psalm 118:1; Psalm 136:1; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; Ezra 3:11; Jeremiah 33:11

a: Who is able to put the LORD's mighty acts into words
p: The Talmud uses this verse to warn against piling up praises of God in prayer.
b: The question is a way of saying no one can praise God enough. The Talmud draws a lesson from it: Rabbi Yochanan said that anyone who goes on and on praising God beyond the fixed words of prayer is "uprooted from the world," since this verse asks who can tell all his praise, meaning only one who could tell all of it should try (Bavli Megillah 18a). The same passage cites Psalm 65:1 (Hebrew 65:2): "For you, God, silence is praise." Christian writers have made a similar point: God is always greater than what is said of him.

a: LORD, keep me in mind with the goodwill you show your people
p: A single "I" prays to share in Israel's restoration. The Greek turns it into "us."
b: Most of the psalm says "we" and "our ancestors." In 106:4–5 one person asks to be remembered when God shows favor to his people, "to look on the good things your chosen ones receive." It is the prayer of someone in exile who longs to see the restoration with his own eyes, like Nehemiah's "My God, remember me for good" (Nehemiah 5:19). The Greek reads "us" (see the variant), making it fit the rest of the psalm. Jesus' companion on the cross asked something similar: "Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingdom" (Luke 23:42).

a: We have sinned along with our ancestors.
p: The same three verbs Solomon gave the exiles to pray (1 Kings 8:47). Daniel and Nehemiah confess alike.
b: Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication imagines Israel in exile, saying: "We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil" (1 Kings 8:47). Psalm 106 uses the same three Hebrew verbs. Daniel 9:5 and Nehemiah 9:16–37 make similar confessions, joining the present generation to its ancestors' sins. Psalm 106 also ends as Solomon's prayer does: God gives his people pity in the eyes of their captors (106:46; 1 Kings 8:50). This is one of the strongest signs that the psalm is a prayer of the exile or soon after.
r: 1 Kings 8:46–50; Daniel 9:5; Nehemiah 9:16–37; Ezra 9:6–7; Leviticus 26:40; Lamentations 5:7

a: and they were defiant at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds
p: Even before the sea split, the people turned on Moses: "Were there no graves in Egypt?" (Exodus 14:11).
b: Exodus 14:10–12 tells how the Israelites, seeing Pharaoh's army behind them, said to Moses, "Were there no graves in Egypt, that you brought us out here to die in the wilderness?" (Exodus 14:11). The psalm counts this as the first act of defiance; its verb, marah, "defy," returns at 106:33 and 106:43. Yam Suf is the Sea of Reeds, called the Red Sea in the Greek and most English Bibles (see the topic page). The Hebrew line is a little rough, "at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds," and both the Greek and some scholars read it differently (see the variant).

a: for the sake of his name
p: God saved Israel not because it deserved it, but for the honor of his name: what he had made known himself to be.
b: Lema'an shemo, "for the sake of his name," means for his reputation among the nations and his own faithfulness to who he is. Moses used this argument when he prayed after the golden calf: "Why let the Egyptians say, 'He brought them out to do them harm'?" (Exodus 32:12). Ezekiel builds a whole chapter on it: God spared Israel in Egypt and the wilderness "for my name's sake, so that it would not be treated as common in the eyes of the nations" (Ezekiel 20:9, a fresh rendering). Psalm 106 and Ezekiel 20 tell Israel's history in very similar ways.
r: Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16; Ezekiel 20:9; Ezekiel 20:14; Ezekiel 20:22; Ezekiel 36:22; Psalm 23:3; Psalm 79:9

a: He scolded the Sea of Reeds, and it went dry
p: God "rebukes" the sea as in Psalm 104:7. Jesus later rebukes the wind and sea in the same way.
b: The verb ga'ar, "scold, rebuke," is the one used for God's command to the waters at creation (Psalm 104:7, "When you scolded them, they ran") and for the drying of the sea in Nahum 1:4 and Isaiah 50:2. Exodus 14:21 gives the means: "All night the LORD made the sea go back by a fierce east wind." The Gospels use the Greek word for "rebuke" when Jesus calms the storm (Mark 4:39), and his disciples ask, "Who can this be? The wind and the sea both do what he says!" (Mark 4:41).
r: Psalm 104:7; Exodus 14:21; Nahum 1:4; Isaiah 50:2; Isaiah 63:13; Mark 4:39–41

a: he redeemed them out of the enemy's power
t: Rescued from the hand of those who hate us
p: Zechariah's song in Luke 1:71 echoes this verse: rescue "from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us."
b: The language is the exodus's: God "redeemed" (ga'al) Israel (Exodus 6:6; Exodus 15:13). Zechariah's song, the Benedictus, uses this verse and 106:45 together when it praises God for "rescue out of our enemies' power and out of the grip of all who hate us," and for keeping in mind "his holy covenant" (Luke 1:71–72, a fresh rendering). The same song opens with the blessing of 106:48 (Luke 1:68).

a: Then they put their trust in his words
p: At the sea the people believed and sang the Song of Moses (Exodus 14:31–15:1). Within days they forgot.
b: Exodus 14:31 says: "They believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant," and then "Moses and the Israelites sang this song" (Exodus 15:1). The psalm grants this, then adds at once: "They were quick to forget" (106:13). Three days later at Marah they complained about the water (Exodus 15:22–24). The pattern of the whole psalm is in these two verses: rescue, a short burst of faith and song, and quick forgetting.

a: In the wilderness they craved and craved
p: The Hebrew says "they craved a craving," the word of Numbers 11, where the place was named "Graves of Craving."
b: Vayyit'avvu ta'avah, "they craved a craving," uses the word of Numbers 11:4: "The hangers-on who were among them were seized by a craving." God sent quail, and "the meat was still between their teeth" when the plague struck (Numbers 11:33), so the place was named Kibroth Hattaavah (Numbers 11:34). Paul uses the story as a warning: these things happened as examples, so that we would not crave evil as they craved (1 Corinthians 10:6). "They tried God" matches Psalm 78:18 and Exodus 17:2; Exodus 17:7.
r: Numbers 11:4; Numbers 11:31–34; Psalm 78:18; Psalm 78:29–31; Exodus 17:7; 1 Corinthians 10:6

a: but he sent a thinning sickness down their throats
p: The KJV has "sent leanness into their soul." The Hebrew means a sickness that thins the body.
b: Razon means leanness or wasting; nefesh here is the throat or appetite that craved meat (compare Numbers 11:6, "our appetite has dried up"; Numbers 11:20). God gave the meat they demanded, and with it a deadly plague (Numbers 11:33). The KJV "sent leanness into their soul" became a preacher's text for spiritual emptiness that follows getting what one wants. That lesson may be true, but the Hebrew describes a sickness in the body. The Greek read the opposite, "fullness" (see the variant).

a: and of Aaron, the LORD's holy one
p: The psalm names Dathan and Abiram but not Korah, perhaps because the sons of Korah were temple singers.
b: Numbers 16 tells of Korah, a Levite, and Dathan and Abiram, Reubenites, who rose against Moses and Aaron. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram's households, and fire consumed 250 men who offered incense (Numbers 16:31–35). Deuteronomy 11:6 also names only Dathan and Abiram. The psalm's silence about Korah may follow that tradition, or may spare the family of the "sons of Korah" whose names head Psalms 42–49 and 84–88. Numbers 26:11 notes that "the sons of Korah did not die." Aaron is "the LORD's holy one" because he was set apart as priest (Exodus 28:36; Numbers 16:5; Numbers 16:7).

a: They made a calf at Horeb
p: Horeb is Deuteronomy's name for Sinai. The psalm tells the golden calf story of Exodus 32.
b: Aaron made "a calf of cast metal," and the people said, "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (Exodus 32:4). The psalm uses massekhah, "cast image," as Exodus does, and Horeb, the name Deuteronomy uses for Sinai (Deuteronomy 9:8). Stephen recalls the calf in Acts 7:41. Jewish tradition counted it the worst sin of Israel's history, whose punishment is felt "in every generation" (Bavli Sanhedrin 102a).

a: They traded their glory
p: Israel gave up its glory, the living God, for a statue of an ox. Paul echoes the line in Romans 1:23.
b: "Their glory" is God himself, Israel's honor and the presence that went with them (compare Jeremiah 2:11: "my people have exchanged their glory for what does not help," a fresh rendering). The bitter detail is that the ox "feeds on grass": they bowed to the image of an animal that has to eat. Paul uses the same words for the whole human race: they "traded the glory of the God who does not decay for the likeness of an image" of humans, birds, animals and reptiles (Romans 1:23, a fresh rendering). Jewish scribal tradition counts this verse among places where the text may once have read "my glory" or "his glory" (see the variant).

a: stood in the broken wall facing him
p: Moses stood like a soldier in a gap in a city wall, holding off the attack, but the attack was God's own anger.
b: Amad bapperets, "he stood in the breach," is a picture from siege warfare: when a wall is broken, a soldier stands in the gap to stop the enemy coming through. Here the one attacking is God, and Moses stands between him and the people. Exodus 32:10–14 and Deuteronomy 9:18–20 tell how Moses pleaded for forty days. Ezekiel uses the same picture: God looked for someone to "stand in the breach before me for the land," and found no one (Ezekiel 22:30; Ezekiel 13:5). The psalm calls Moses "his chosen one" (bechiro), the only time this title is used of him.
r: Exodus 32:10–14; Exodus 32:30–32; Deuteronomy 9:18–20; Ezekiel 22:30; Ezekiel 13:5; Jeremiah 15:1

a: They rejected the land worth wanting
p: Numbers 13–14: after the spies' bad report, the people wept and wanted to go back to Egypt.
b: "The land worth wanting" (erets chemdah, "land of delight") is the land of Jeremiah 3:19 and Zechariah 7:14. The spies called it "a land that eats up the people who live there" (Numbers 13:32), and the people complained "in their tents" (106:25; Deuteronomy 1:27). God said, "How long will they not believe in me, after all the signs I have done among them?" (Numbers 14:11). Hebrews 3:7–4:11 uses this failure, with Psalm 95, to warn Christians not to fall short of God's rest through unbelief.

a: So he lifted his hand to them in an oath
p: To raise the hand was to swear an oath. God swore that the wilderness generation would die there.
b: God says in Numbers 14:30 that none of them will enter "the land where I raised my hand to settle you," and in Numbers 14:28–29 he swears that their bodies will fall in the wilderness. The raised hand was the gesture of an oath (Genesis 14:22; Exodus 6:8). Psalm 106:27 adds a second oath, to scatter their descendants among the nations, which the Torah does not attach to this event. Ezekiel 20:23 says the same: "I lifted my hand to them in the wilderness to scatter them among the nations" (a fresh rendering). The psalm thus reads the exile as foretold long before.
r: Numbers 14:28–30; Ezekiel 20:15; Ezekiel 20:23; Genesis 14:22; Exodus 6:8; Leviticus 26:33; Deuteronomy 28:64

a: and ate the sacrifices of the dead
p: The "dead" may be lifeless idols, or the dead who were honored with funeral feasts. Numbers 25 tells the story.
b: At Shittim, Moabite women "invited the people to the sacrifices for their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods. So Israel tied itself to the Baal of Peor" (Numbers 25:2–3). The psalm calls the meals "sacrifices of the dead." Many read "the dead" as a mocking name for idols, which have no life (compare Psalm 115:4–7), and the Greek kept "of the dead" (nekrōn). Others think it means a cult of the dead, meals for dead ancestors, which archaeology and texts from Ugarit (the marzeach feast) show were known in Canaan; Deuteronomy 26:14 forbids offering tithe "to the dead." Rashi took it as offerings to idols, which are like the dead.
r: Numbers 25:1–3; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 26:14; Hosea 9:10; Psalm 115:4–7; 1 Corinthians 10:8

a: But Phinehas rose and gave judgment
p: Yefallel means to judge, decide or intervene. It describes Phinehas' spear thrust in Numbers 25 in a neutral word.
b: Phinehas killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman with one spear, and the plague stopped (Numbers 25:7–8). The psalm does not describe the killing. It uses vayfallel, a verb related to tefillah, "prayer," which in the Piel means to judge or arbitrate (1 Samuel 2:25; Ezekiel 16:52). So Phinehas "executed judgment" or "intervened." The Targum and some rabbinic readers took it as "he prayed"; the Greek has "he made atonement" (exilasato), matching Numbers 25:13, "made atonement for the Israelites."

a: It was reckoned to him as righteousness
p: The same words describe Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6. Here they are said of Phinehas' zeal.
b: Vattechashev lo litsdaqah repeats the key words of Genesis 15:6: "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." These are the only two places in the Hebrew Bible with this phrase. For Abraham it is faith; for Phinehas it is a deed of zeal, rewarded with "a covenant of priesthood for all time" (Numbers 25:13). Paul builds on Genesis 15:6 (Romans 4:3), James on Abraham's deeds (James 2:21–23), and 1 Maccabees 2:52 joins the two: Abraham's faithfulness in testing "was reckoned to him as righteousness," with Phinehas named in the next verses (1 Maccabees 2:54). See the chapter page for how the churches read it.
r: Genesis 15:6; Numbers 25:11–13; Romans 4:3; Romans 4:9–10; James 2:21–23; 1 Maccabees 2:52; 1 Maccabees 2:54; Galatians 3:6

a: At the waters of Meribah they stirred up his anger
t: Why Moses did not enter the land
p: Moses struck the rock at Meribah and was barred from the land. The psalm blames the people.
b: At Meribah the community quarreled, and Moses said, "Listen, please, you rebels! Are we to bring water out of this rock for you?" (Numbers 20:10).
