God told Moses and Aaron, "You did not believe me, to treat me as holy" (Numbers 20:12). Deuteronomy has Moses say three times that the LORD was angry with him "because of you" (Deuteronomy 1:37; Deuteronomy 3:26; Deuteronomy 4:21), and the psalm agrees: "Moses came to harm on their account." Jewish commentators have long debated what exactly Moses' sin was: striking instead of speaking, his anger, or his words "Are we to bring water."
r: Numbers 20:2–13; Numbers 20:24; Numbers 27:14; Deuteronomy 1:37; Deuteronomy 3:26; Deuteronomy 32:51

a: for they defied his spirit
p: "His spirit" may be God's Spirit (as in Isaiah 63:10) or Moses' own spirit, which the people embittered.
b: If "his" means God, the people rebelled against God's Spirit, as Isaiah 63:10 says of the wilderness generation: "they turned rebel and pained his holy spirit" (a fresh rendering). If "his" means Moses, the people provoked Moses' spirit until he "let careless words slip from his lips." The Greek has "they embittered his spirit," which fits Moses better, and many Jewish commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) take it so. The Plain keeps the ambiguous "his." Bitta, "speak rashly," is the word for a careless oath in Leviticus 5:4.
orig: כִּי־הִמְרוּ אֶת־רוּחוֹ וַיְבַטֵּא בִּשְׂפָתָיו (ki-himru et-rucho vayvatte bisfatav)

a: They did not wipe out the peoples
p: The psalm blames Israel for not destroying the Canaanites, as Deuteronomy 7 commanded. Modern readers find this hard.
b: Deuteronomy 7:1–5 and Numbers 33:52–55 command Israel to drive out or destroy the peoples of Canaan, and Judges 1:21–36 and Judges 2:1–3 record that they did not. The psalm, like Judges, says the result was Israel's own corruption (106:35–36). Jewish and Christian readers have long struggled with this command. Many explain that its real target was the idolatry and child sacrifice named in 106:37–38, that the language of total destruction is partly a war rhetoric of the time, or that it applied to one moment and not to any later war. See the topic on holy war.

a: and those became a trap for them
p: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua and Judges all warn that Canaan's gods would become a trap for Israel.
b: Moqesh is a bait trap for birds. The warnings are many: Exodus 23:33 and Exodus 34:12, Deuteronomy 7:16, Joshua 23:13 and Judges 2:3 ("their gods will become a trap for you"). Judges 8:27 says Gideon's ephod "became a trap" to his family. The psalm reports that the warning came true.
r: Exodus 23:33; Exodus 34:12; Deuteronomy 7:16; Joshua 23:13; Judges 2:3; Judges 8:27

a: They offered up their own sons
p: Israelites sacrificed their own children to the gods of Canaan, as Kings, Jeremiah and Ezekiel also report.
b: The prophets and Kings name the practice: Ahaz and Manasseh made their sons "pass through the fire" (2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6), and Jeremiah condemns the Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where people burned their sons and daughters (Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5). Ezekiel 16:20–21 and Ezekiel 23:37 accuse Jerusalem of slaughtering its children. The word for the gods here is shedim, "demons," used elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:17: "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God." Paul echoes that verse in 1 Corinthians 10:20. Excavations at Carthage, a Phoenician colony, found thousands of urns of burned infants, which most archaeologists take as evidence of the same kind of rite.
r: Deuteronomy 32:17; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5; Ezekiel 16:20–21; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Leviticus 18:21

a: and the land was defiled with bloodshed
p: Numbers 35:33 warns that bloodshed pollutes the land. Innocent children's blood made the land itself unclean.
b: Vattechenaf ha'arets badamim: "the land was polluted with blood." The verb chanaf is used of a land made unclean by murder in Numbers 35:33: "Do not pollute the land you live in. Blood pollutes the land"; it is also used of a land defiled by unfaithfulness in Jeremiah 3:1–2; Jeremiah 3:9. In the Torah, a land defiled this way "vomits out" its people (Leviticus 18:24–28), so the psalm prepares for the exile that follows (106:41).

a: and were unfaithful like a prostitute in their practices
p: The prophets picture Israel's idolatry as a wife's unfaithfulness. The verb zanah means to act as a prostitute.
b: Judges 2:17 says the Israelites "went after other gods like a prostitute," and Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel build the picture into whole chapters (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16; Ezekiel 23). The point is not sexual sin in itself but broken covenant: God is the husband, Israel the wife who went after other lovers. The same image turns hopeful when God promises to win her back (Hosea 2:14–20).

a: Again and again he pulled them out
p: 106:40–46 sums up the book of Judges: sin, anger, oppression, a cry for help, and rescue, over and over.
b: Judges 2:11–19 sets out the same cycle: the Israelites served the Baals, the LORD's anger blazed and "He put them in the power of raiders" (Judges 2:14), they groaned, he raised up judges and rescued them, and "Once the judge was dead, they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors" (Judges 2:19). Nehemiah 9:26–31 tells it the same way. The psalm compresses centuries, from the judges to the exile, into a few lines and ends with the exile itself, "all who had taken them captive" (106:46).

a: and changed his mind
p: Nicham means to change one's mind or feel sorrow. God "relents" from punishment because of his loyal love.
b: Vayyinnachem is used of God changing his mind about punishing, as after the golden calf (Exodus 32:14, "the LORD changed his mind about the harm") and in Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2, where the creed of Exodus 34:6 adds "and relents from harm." 1 Samuel 15:29 says God does not change his mind like a human. Theologians reconcile the two by saying God's purpose of mercy is constant, while his announced judgments are often conditional (Jeremiah 18:7–10). See the topic page on God's regret.
r: Exodus 32:14; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Jeremiah 18:7–10; 1 Samuel 15:29; Amos 7:3

a: He let them find pity
t: Pity in the eyes of captors
p: This is Solomon's prayer for the exiles answered: "Let their captors look on them with pity" (1 Kings 8:50).
b: Solomon prayed: "Let their captors look on them with pity and treat them with pity" (1 Kings 8:50). The psalm says God did it. Readers think of the kindness of the Babylonian king to Jehoiachin (2 Kings 25:27–30), of Cyrus' decree (Ezra 1:1–4), of Nehemiah finding favor with Artaxerxes (Nehemiah 1:11; Nehemiah 2:8), and of Daniel and Esther. The verse shows the psalm's setting: the people are still "among the nations" (106:47).
r: 1 Kings 8:50; 2 Kings 25:27–30; Ezra 1:1–4; Nehemiah 1:11; Nehemiah 2:8; Daniel 1:9; Jeremiah 42:12

a: and gather us from the nations
p: The psalm ends asking to be gathered from the nations. Chronicles gives the prayer to David's singers.
b: "Gather us" assumes Israel is scattered, the situation of Deuteronomy 30:3–4 and Jeremiah 29:14, where God promises to gather his people from all the nations. 1 Chronicles 16:35 quotes the verse with small changes: "Rescue us, God who rescues us! / Gather us and pull us out from the nations." Chronicles has "God who rescues us" for "LORD our God" and adds "pull us out" (hatsilenu). Placing an exiles' prayer at David's ark festival shows how Chronicles wrote for its own post-exile readers. Jews still pray daily, in the Amidah, for God to "gather us together from the four corners of the earth."
r: 1 Chronicles 16:35; Deuteronomy 30:3–4; Jeremiah 29:14; Isaiah 43:5–6; Ezekiel 36:24; Nehemiah 1:9

a: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
p: This blessing closes the fourth of the Psalter's five books, as Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19 and Psalm 89:52 close the first three.
b: Each of the first four books of Psalms ends with a doxology, a short blessing of God: Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52 and here. Psalm 150 as a whole closes Book V. 106:48 is the only one that tells the people to answer, "Amen!" and adds "Praise the LORD!" 1 Chronicles 16:36 quotes the verse and turns the command into a report: "And the whole people said, 'Amen!' and gave praise to the LORD." Many scholars take this as evidence that Book IV ended here by the time Chronicles was written, about 400–300 BC. Zechariah's song opens with the same blessing (Luke 1:68). Book IV (90–106) begins with Moses (Psalm 90) and ends by retelling Moses' generation.
r: Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 150:1–6; 1 Chronicles 16:36; Luke 1:68; Psalm 90:0

a: And let all the people say, "Amen!"
p: Amen means "so be it," "it is true." The Greek translated it "So be it, so be it."
b: Amen comes from the root of emunah, "faithfulness, firmness." The people say it to accept a curse, blessing or prayer as their own (Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6). The Greek Psalter translates it genoito genoito, "so be it, so be it," as at the ends of Books I to III. Christians kept the Hebrew word, as the New Testament does (1 Corinthians 14:16; Revelation 5:14), and still say it at the end of prayers.
r: Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6; 1 Chronicles 16:36; 1 Corinthians 14:16; Revelation 5:14; 2 Corinthians 1:20
